parts.title: Campus Conversation: Returning a Textbook
script: Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at the campus bookstore.
Hi. Yes, I want to return this textbook. I bought it last week for my history class.
OK. Is there a problem with the book?
No, the book is fine. But I changed my class. I am not taking history this semester. Now I am taking art.
I see. Do you have your receipt?
Thank you. Let me look... You bought it eight days ago. That's good. You can return books for a full refund within fourteen days.
Oh, great. I was worried it was too late.
No, you're fine. But wait. I need to check the book. Did you write in it?
Well... I wrote my name on the first page. Is that a problem?
Hmm, just your name? That's OK. We can't take books with a lot of notes or highlighting, but a name is fine.
Phew. OK. How will I get my money back?
You paid with a credit card, so the money will go back to your card. It takes about three to five days.
That's fine. Also, I need a book for my new art class. Do you have it?
Let me check the computer... Yes, we have it. It's on the second floor, near the stairs. And there are used copies too. They are cheaper.
Used copies? Perfect. I'll go look now. Thanks for your help!

questions.q: Why does the student go to the bookstore?
o: To pay for an art class
questions.exp: She says, 'I want to return this textbook.'

questions.q: Why does the student want to return the book?
questions.exp: She says, 'I changed my class. I am not taking history this semester.'

questions.q: How many days do students have to return a book for a full refund?
questions.exp: The man says, 'You can return books for a full refund within fourteen days.'

questions.q: Listen again: "Well... I wrote my name on the first page. Is that a problem?" Why does the student say this?
o: She is worried the bookstore will not take the book
She wants the man to write his name too
She is proud of her handwriting
She wants to keep the book
questions.exp: She is not sure if writing her name is OK, so she is worried they will not accept the book.

questions.q: How will the student get her money back?
o: The money will go back to her credit card
As a gift card for the bookstore
By a check in the mail
questions.exp: The man says, 'The money will go back to your card.'

questions.q: What will the student probably do next?
o: Go to the second floor to look for a used art book
questions.exp: The man says the book is on the second floor and used copies are cheaper. She says, 'I'll go look now.'

parts.title: Academic Lecture: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
script: Listen to part of a lecture in an earth science class.
Good morning, everyone. Let's start with a simple question. Have you ever tasted ocean water? It's very salty, right? You can't drink it. Today we will talk about why the ocean is salty.
Here's something surprising. Most of the salt in the ocean comes from rocks on land. Let me explain how.

First, it rains. Rain water is a little bit acidic. That means it can slowly break down rocks. When rain falls on rocks, it takes very small pieces of minerals from them. Salt is one of these minerals.
Next, the rain water goes into rivers. The rivers carry the salt to the ocean. River water has salt too, but only a very small amount, so it doesn't taste salty.

Then, the sun heats the ocean. Water evaporates. That means it changes into gas and goes up into the air. But the salt does not go up. The salt stays in the ocean. This has happened for millions of years, so the salt slowly built up.

There is also a second source of salt: the ocean floor. At the bottom of the ocean, there are openings where hot water and minerals come out from inside the Earth. These openings also add salt to the ocean.

Now, how salty is the ocean? On average, about three and a half percent of ocean water is salt. If you took all the salt out of the oceans and put it on land, it would cover all the land with a layer about one hundred and sixty meters high. That's taller than a forty-story building!
Some places are saltier than others. The Dead Sea, for example, is so salty that people can float on top of the water easily. Next class, we will look at why the Dead Sea is so salty.

questions.q: What is the lecture mainly about?
questions.exp: The professor says, 'Today we will talk about why the ocean is salty.'

questions.q: According to the professor, where does most of the salt in the ocean come from?
questions.exp: She says, 'Most of the salt in the ocean comes from rocks on land.'

questions.q: Why doesn't river water taste salty?
o: River water has only a very small amount of salt
Rain removes the salt from rivers
questions.exp: She says river water has 'only a very small amount, so it doesn't taste salty.'

questions.q: What happens to the salt when ocean water evaporates?
o: It goes up into the air
It goes back to the rivers
questions.exp: She says, 'The salt does not go up. The salt stays in the ocean.'

questions.q: Listen again: "Have you ever tasted ocean water? It's very salty, right?" Why does the professor say this?
o: To ask students to taste ocean water in class
To introduce the topic with something students know
To say that ocean water is good to drink
To check if students went to the beach
questions.exp: She starts with a common experience to introduce the topic of why the ocean is salty.

questions.q: How does the professor explain how salt gets into the ocean?
o: She describes the steps in order: rain, rivers, then evaporation
She tells a story about her trip
She lists the names of famous scientists
questions.exp: She uses 'First... Next... Then...' to describe the steps in order.
